Four beginner-friendly sewn pouches and bags — each with pictures for every stage of the build.

Project 1 · Sewing

Mini Travel Jewelry Organizer

Green gingham outside, pink floral printed lining inside. Three curved pockets stacked down the length, a rounded top, plastic snap closure, and a fabric tab with a split key ring. Fold it up and it’s palm-sized.

Finished look: Panel 6, belowTrue pocket layout: Panel 5

Storyboard — the whole build at a glance

What you need

About measurements: the exact cut measurements were shown on-screen in the original video only and are not listed here, rather than guessed.

Fabric & hardware

  • Fabric for 2 main-body pieces
  • Fabric for 3 pocket pieces
  • A small fabric strip for the key-ring tab
  • Light-to-medium weight iron-on interfacing — for the 2 main-body pieces only, not the pockets
  • Plastic snap set with snap pliers
  • Split key ring

Tools

  • Sewing machine
  • Iron
  • Scissors
  • Sewing clips
  • Pencil for marking
  • Quilting ruler, if you have one
  • Chopstick or point turner — for pushing out seams

How to make it

Follow in order. The fiddly parts are the small curves, turning out the tiny pockets, and placing the second snap — go slow on those.

  1. Iron on the interfacing

    Iron interfacing onto both main-body pieces. This gives the pouch its body so it isn’t floppy. Pockets don’t get interfacing.

  2. Make the key-ring tab

    Fold the strip in half and press. Fold both raw edges into the center and press. Fold in half again, then sew down both long sides.

  3. Mark the curves

    Mark curved guidelines on 1 main-body piece and on all 3 pockets.

  4. Sew each pocket

    Right sides together, sew the curve — backstitch at the start and stop, and go slow. Sew straight across the bottom and leave the sides open. Trim and notch the curve without cutting the stitches, turn it out, finger-press, then iron.

  5. Attach the pockets

    Place the pockets on the unmarked main-body piece, eyeballed even with a little space at the bottom. Sew only across the bottom edge of each pocket — that’s what leaves it open at the top.

  6. Assemble the pouch

    Fold the tab in half and place it on the outside of the top pocket. Lay the marked main-body piece on top, marked side up, and clip. Sew the sides and top with about a ¼″ seam, leaving the bottom open.

  7. Turn it right-side out

    Trim and notch the top curve, turn the pouch right-side out through the bottom, push out the seams and corners with a chopstick, and press well.

  8. Topstitch all the way around

    Tuck the raw bottom edge in, clip, and topstitch around the whole edge — this closes the bottom. Go slow over the bulky corners.

  9. Add the snaps

    Fold the top in half to mark the center for the first snap. Then fold the pouch up closed to mark where the mating snap goes.

    The second snap must go inside the top pocket, not over it — or the pocket won’t open.

  10. Add the key ring — done

    Thread the split key ring through the tab. Fold it up, snap it shut, and it’s ready to use.

Project 2 · Sewing

Structured Zippered Pouch — Plaid

A structured — not floppy — rectangular zippered pouch in red, white and black plaid, with a cream lining, a red zipper down the center, small red fabric tabs at the zipper ends, and a red handle. Shown filled with headphones and a water bottle to show the capacity.

Cut size: 45 cm × 35 cmPattern marked “5”

Storyboard — the build in pictures

1Steps 1–2 — Cut & clip. Plaid over cream lining on the mat, both cut together to the pattern marked “5” (45 cm × 35 cm), then clipped together.
2Step 3 — Zipper. The red zipper sewn down the center between the layers.
3Step 5 — Tabs. Small red fabric tabs added at the zipper ends.
4Step 6 — Boxy sides. Sides folded and sewn to form the structured, boxy shape.
5Step 7 — Handle. The red handle attached.
6Step 8 — Finished. Bag opened to show the cream interior — sized for headphones and a water bottle.

What you need

About the stiffening: this pouch holds its shape, but the stiffening that makes it structured was not named in the original video, so no specific stiffener is listed here as the original maker’s. You will need some way to give it body — a fabric store can advise on a suitable option for a structured pouch.

Fabric & hardware

  • Plaid exterior fabric — red, white and black
  • Cream lining fabric
  • Exterior and lining cut together: 45 cm × 35 cm, pattern marked “5”
  • Red zipper
  • Red fabric for the zipper-end tabs and the handle

Tools

  • Sewing machine
  • Cutting mat
  • Sewing clips
  • Scissors

How to make it

Follow in order — the storyboard above matches these steps panel by panel.

  1. Cut both layers together

    Lay the plaid exterior over the cream lining on a cutting mat and cut both layers together using the pattern marked “5” — 45 cm × 35 cm.

  2. Clip the layers together

    Clip the exterior and lining together so they feed through the machine as one piece.

  3. Sew the zipper down the center

    Sew the red zipper down the center between the layers.

  4. Turn it right-side out

    Turn the piece right-side out so the plaid faces out and the cream lining sits inside.

  5. Add the zipper-end tabs

    Add the small red fabric tabs at the zipper ends.

  6. Form the boxy shape

    Fold and sew the sides to form the boxy, structured shape.

  7. Attach the handle

    Attach the red handle.

  8. Shape it — done

    Turn and shape the finished bag, then open it to show the cream interior.

Project 3 · Sewing

Green Floral Boxy Pencil Pouch

Rectangular boxy pencil pouches in white fabric with a green and blue floral pattern and a gold metal zipper — no lining. Four finished pouches are shown in the original project.

Makes 4, as shownNo liningBoxed corners

Storyboard — the build in pictures

1Step 1 — Zipper on. The gold metal zipper aligned with the floral fabric and stitched on.
2Step 2 — Second piece. The second piece of fabric attached to form the pouch body.
3Step 3 — Boxed corners. Side seams sewn, with the boxed corners formed.
4Step 4 — Trim. Excess material trimmed away.
5Step 5 — Turn & shape. Pouch turned right-side out and shaped.
6Finished. The 4 completed pouches.

What you need

About measurements: exact fabric measurements and zipper length were not retrieved from the original video, so none are listed here rather than guessed.

Fabric & hardware

  • White fabric with a green and blue floral pattern — 2 pieces per pouch
  • Gold metal zipper — one per pouch
  • No lining on this design

Tools

  • Sewing machine
  • Scissors — for trimming
From similar pouches: in similar no-lining pouches, cotton with fusible interfacing is used. That is background from similar pouches, not confirmed for this floral pouch.

How to make it

Follow in order — the storyboard above matches these steps panel by panel.

  1. Stitch the zipper to the fabric

    Align the metal zipper with the floral fabric and stitch it on.

  2. Attach the second piece

    Attach the second piece of fabric to form the pouch body.

  3. Sew the sides and box the corners

    Sew the side seams, including forming the boxed corners that give the pouch its boxy shape.

  4. Trim the excess

    Trim excess material.

  5. Turn and shape — done

    Turn the pouch right-side out and shape it. Repeat for as many as you want — four are shown.

Project 4 · Sewing

DIY Makeup Bag — Blue Checkered

A small rectangular boxy makeup bag: blue-and-white small checkered cotton on the outside, a light blue lining with a small dark pattern inside, a black zipper across the top with silver pulls, and a black woven webbing handle strap. An easy beginner project — at the end it’s shown filled with makeup to show how much it holds.

Cut size: 35 cm × 50 cmZipper: 35 cmBeginner friendly

Storyboard — the build in pictures

1Step 1 — Cut. The checkered outer fabric cut to 35 × 50 cm, with the light blue lining cut to match.
2Step 2 — Notched shape. The fabric folded and cut into the bag shape, with the corner notches that later form the boxy base.
3Step 3 — Zipper. The black zipper sewn to the top and bottom edges of the outer fabric.
4Steps 4–5 — Lining & trim. The lining attached, then excess fabric and zipper ends trimmed away.
5Steps 6–7 — Handle & box shape. The black webbing handle added, and the side seams sewn to form the box shape.
6Step 8 — Finished. The bag turned right-side out and zipped — shown open and filled with makeup to show the capacity.

What you need

About the details that aren’t published: the exact notch sizes and positions and the seam allowances are not published with this project, so they aren’t listed here rather than guessed. No interfacing or stiffener is confirmed for this bag either — none is listed, and the bag’s body comes from the fabric and the boxed construction.

Fabric & hardware

  • Outer fabric — blue-and-white small checkered cotton, cut 35 × 50 cm
  • Lining fabric — light blue with a small dark pattern, cut the same size, 35 × 50 cm
  • Black zipper — 35 cm, with silver pulls
  • Black woven strap / webbing — for the handle
  • Matching thread

Tools

  • Sewing machine
  • Scissors
  • Sewing clips or pins
  • Ruler and marking tool
  • Iron

How to make it

Follow in order — the storyboard above matches these steps panel by panel.

  1. Cut the outer fabric and lining

    Lay out the blue-and-white checkered cotton and cut the outer piece to 35 × 50 cm. Cut the light blue lining piece to match.

  2. Cut the notched bag shape

    Fold the fabric and cut it into the bag shape, cutting the corner notches — those notches are what later form the boxy base.

  3. Sew on the zipper

    Sew the 35 cm black zipper to the top and bottom edges of the outer fabric.

  4. Attach the lining

    Attach the light blue lining piece so it sits inside the bag.

  5. Trim the excess

    Trim away the excess fabric and the zipper ends for a neat finish.

  6. Add the handle

    Add the black woven webbing strap as the handle.

  7. Sew the side seams

    Sew the side seams to close the bag and form its box shape.

  8. Turn it out — done

    Turn the bag right-side out, zip it closed, and it’s ready. Fill it with makeup to see the finished capacity.
